claim: Hgf transcripts were induced 10–500-fold with a time course that peaked 2–3 days after injury in murine tibialis anterior muscle tissue.

claim: After injury, a 65% reduction in stem cell numbers was present at 20 dpi in TxFanMet animals compared to control animals.

claim: Various cytokines, among them interleukin-1 and interleukin-6, activate HGF transcription, which might account for the increased HGF transcripts observed after tissue damage.
source: In addition, various cytokines, among them interleukin-1 and interleukin-6, activate HGF transcription, which might account for the increased HGF transcripts observed after tissue damage (Birchmeier et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Loss of Met impairs the resistance of muscle stem cells against acute inflammation.
source: We demonstrate here that loss of Met impairs the resistance of muscle stem cells against acute inflammation.
evidence: Inferred from the increased apoptosis and reduced stem cell numbers in Met mutants

claim: In vivo the additional loss of Cxcr4 exacerbated the deficits observed after loss of Met.
source: Moreover, in vivo the additional loss of Cxcr4 exacerbated the deficits observed after loss of Met.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of single and double mutant phenotypes

claim: The cooperative effect detected in vivo is reflected by the fact that both receptors, Met and Cxcr4, use in part overlapping downstream signaling cascades but also activate distinct signaling molecules.
source: The cooperative effect that we detected here in vivo is reflected by the fact that both receptors, Met and Cxcr4, use in part overlapping downstream signaling cascades but also activate distinct signaling molecules.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of signaling pathways

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation of MET results in the activation of various signaling events that regulate cell motility, proliferation, and survival; among them RAS/MAPK, PI3-kinase/AKT, PLCγ/PKC, RAC/CDC42, and CRK.
source: Tyrosine phosphorylation of MET results in the activation of various signaling events that regulate cell motility, proliferation, and survival; among them RAS/MAPK, PI3-kinase/AKT, PLCγ/PKC, RAC/CDC42, and CRK (Birchmeier et al., 2003; Gentile et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: CXCR4 uses G-proteins to transmit signals into the cytoplasm, which involves activation of second messenger-regulated serine/threonine kinases or ion channels.
source: CXCR4 uses G-proteins to transmit signals into the cytoplasm, which involves activation of second messenger-regulated serine/threonine kinases or ion channels.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge

claim: CXCR4 also activates RAS/MAPK, PI3-kinase/AKT, and CRK signaling, which is particularly well documented in cancer cells.
source: However, CXCR4 also activates RAS/MAPK, PI3-kinase/AKT, and CRK signaling, which is particularly well documented in cancer cells (Teicher and Fricker, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Among these cascades, PI3-kinase/AKT is well known to act anti-apoptotically.
source: Among these cascades, PI3-kinase/AKT is well known to act anti-apoptotically, and MAPK/ERK signals can counteract the apoptotic activity of TNFα (Tran et al., 2001; Franke et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: MAPK/ERK signals can counteract the apoptotic activity of TNFα.
source: Among these cascades, PI3-kinase/AKT is well known to act anti-apoptotically, and MAPK/ERK signals can counteract the apoptotic activity of TNFα (Tran et al., 2001; Franke et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: TNFα is one of many pro-inflammatory cytokines that are rapidly induced upon acute muscle injury.
source: TNFα is one of many pro-inflammatory cytokines that are rapidly induced upon acute muscle injury, and TNFα is highly expressed by pro-inflammatory macrophages.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1A and established knowledge

claim: TNFα is highly expressed by pro-inflammatory macrophages.
source: TNFα is one of many pro-inflammatory cytokines that are rapidly induced upon acute muscle injury, and TNFα is highly expressed by pro-inflammatory macrophages.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge

claim: The primary role of TNFα is to regulate immune cells.
source: The primary role of TNFα is to regulate immune cells, but it also affects the proliferation and differentiation of cultured muscle cells (Wallach et al., 1999; Li, 2003; Luo et al., 2005; Palacios et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: TNFα affects the proliferation and differentiation of cultured muscle cells.
source: The primary role of TNFα is to regulate immune cells, but it also affects the proliferation and differentiation of cultured muscle cells (Wallach et al., 1999; Li, 2003; Luo et al., 2005; Palacios et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Mice lacking TNFα receptors p55 and p75 show that TNFα does not play an essential role in muscle regeneration, indicating that this cytokine seems to act redundantly with other factors.
source: Mice lacking TNFα receptors p55 and p75 show that TNFα does not play an essential role in muscle regeneration, indicating that this cytokine seems to act redundantly with other factors (Collins and Grounds, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Systemic injection of TNFα neutralizing antibodies protected dystrophic skeletal muscle of mdx mice from necrosis and increased the number of PAX7+ cells.
source: However, systemic injection of TNFα neutralizing antibodies protected dystrophic skeletal muscle of mdx mice from necrosis and increased the number of PAX7+ cells (Palacios et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: TNFα exacerbates muscle fiber damage and impairs muscle stem cell maintenance in dystrophic muscle.
source: This indicates that TNFα exacerbates muscle fiber damage and, in addition, impairs muscle stem cell maintenance in dystrophic muscle.
evidence: Inferred from the protective effect of TNFα neutralizing antibodies in mdx mice

claim: TNFα signals are damaging for muscle stem cells during acute inflammation after injury.
source: Our analysis indicates that TNFα signals are also damaging for muscle stem cells during acute inflammation after injury, but that endogenous HGF and CXCL12 may counteract this.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of apoptosis by TNFα neutralizing antibodies

claim: Endogenous HGF and CXCL12 may counteract the damaging effects of TNFα on muscle stem cells during acute inflammation after injury.
source: Our analysis indicates that TNFα signals are also damaging for muscle stem cells during acute inflammation after injury, but that endogenous HGF and CXCL12 may counteract this.
evidence: Inferred from the increased apoptosis in mutants lacking Met and Cxcr4 and rescue by TNFα neutralization

claim: Effects of TNFα are modulated by other signals, and particularly MAPK/ERK activity can override the apoptotic TNFα signal.
source: Effects of TNFα are modulated by other signals, and particularly MAPK/ERK activity can override the apoptotic TNFα signal (Tran et al., 2001; Aggarwal, 2003; Wada and Penninger, 2004; Lu and Xu, 2006; Lau et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Acute skeletal muscle injury resulting in inflammation is a common clinical condition caused by trauma, severe contraction, chemicals, myotoxins, and ischemia.
source: Acute skeletal muscle injury resulting in inflammation is a common clinical condition caused by trauma, severe contraction, chemicals, myotoxins, and ischemia.
evidence: Statement of established clinical knowledge

claim: Acute inflammation is observed in muscle diseases like dystrophy.
source: Similarly, acute inflammation is observed in muscle diseases like dystrophy (Kharraz et al., 2014; Tidball et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: HGF/MET and CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling protects muscle stem cells against the noxious environment generated by the inflammatory response.
source: Our genetic experiments indicate that HGF/MET and CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling protects muscle stem cells against the noxious environment generated by the inflammatory response.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic experiments showing increased apoptosis in mutants and rescue by TNFα neutralization

claim: Exogenous HGF was previously tested in muscle injury and increased the numbers of activated muscle stem cells, but did not enhance fiber growth.
source: Exogenous HGF was previously tested in muscle injury and increased the numbers of activated muscle stem cells, but did not enhance fiber growth (Miller et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: In healthy muscle, endogenous factors, among them HGF, suffice to ensure appropriate regeneration.
source: Thus, in healthy muscle, endogenous factors, among them HGF, suffice to ensure appropriate regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that exogenous HGF did not enhance fiber growth

claim: In muscle disease where repair mechanisms fail, enhanced cyto-protection of muscle stem cells appears to be beneficial.
source: Nevertheless, in muscle disease where repair mechanisms fail, enhanced cyto-protection of muscle stem cells appears to be beneficial (Palacios et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature showing benefit of TNFα neutralization in mdx mice

claim: Whether HGF/MET and CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling protects against TNFα-induced damage in muscle disease settings will need further investigation.
source: Whether HGF/MET and CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling protects against TNFα-induced damage in such disease settings will need further investigation.
evidence: Statement about future research needs

claim: Inflammatory cells are needed to remove the debris at the site of injury and provide signals that are beneficial for repair.
source: Inflammatory cells are needed to remove the debris at the site of injury and provide signals that are beneficial for repair.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge from the abstract

claim: Inflammatory cells release chemokines, reactive oxygen species, as well as enzymes for clearance of damaged cells and fibers, which muscle stem cells have to withstand in order to regenerate the muscle.
source: However, they also release chemokines, reactive oxygen species, as well as enzymes for clearance of damaged cells and fibers, which muscle stem cells have to withstand in order to regenerate the muscle.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge from the abstract

claim: MET and CXCR4 cooperate to protect muscle stem cells against the adverse environment encountered during muscle repair.
source: We show here that MET and CXCR4 cooperate to protect muscle stem cells against the adverse environment encountered during muscle repair.
evidence: Main finding of the study, supported by genetic experiments

claim: The powerful cyto-protective role of MET and CXCR4 was revealed by the genetic ablation of Met and Cxcr4 in muscle stem cells of mice, which resulted in severe apoptosis during early stages of regeneration.
source: This powerful cyto-protective role was revealed by the genetic ablation of Met and Cxcr4 in muscle stem cells of mice, which resulted in severe apoptosis during early stages of regeneration.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data in Figure 6

claim: TNFα neutralizing antibodies rescued the apoptosis in Met and Cxcr4 mutant muscle stem cells, indicating that TNFα provides crucial cell-death signals during muscle repair that are counteracted by MET and CXCR4.
source: TNFα neutralizing antibodies rescued the apoptosis, indicating that TNFα provides crucial cell-death signals during muscle repair that are counteracted by MET and CXCR4.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 7

claim: Muscle stem cells require MET and CXCR4 to protect them against the harsh inflammatory environment encountered in an acute muscle injury.
source: We conclude that muscle stem cells require MET and CXCR4 to protect them against the harsh inflammatory environment encountered in an acute muscle injury.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study, inferred from all experimental data

claim: Inflammatory factors have dual effects, damaging (TNFα) and protecting (HGF and CXCL12) muscle stem cells during acute injury and regeneration.
source: Together, our study shows that inflammatory factors have dual effects, damaging (TNFα) and protecting (HGF and CXCL12) muscle stem cells during acute injury and regeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the combined effects of TNFα-induced apoptosis and HGF/CXCL12-mediated protection
